meta.title: Heritage of Africa - states and kingdoms of the African past
meta.note: Extents are approximate scholarly reconstructions at each polity's height, authored for this project from open scholarship; they are political watersheds, not surveyed borders. Negative years are BCE.
sources: UNESCO General History of Africa, vols. I–VIII (1981–1993)
J. F. Ade Ajayi & Michael Crowder (eds.), Historical Atlas of Africa (1985)
John Iliffe, Africans: The History of a Continent (3rd ed., 2017)

polities.name: Old Kingdom Egypt
polities.note: The pyramid age. A unified Nile state ruled from Memphis, whose god-kings commanded the surplus of the floodplain to raise Giza and Saqqara, and whose expeditions reached Byblos and Nubia.
sources: Shaw, Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

polities.name: New Kingdom Egypt
polities.note: Egypt at imperial reach: Thutmose III and Ramesses II pushed the frontier south past the Fourth Cataract and north into Syria, and Nubian gold underwrote the temples of Karnak.

polities.name: Kingdom of Kerma
polities.note: The first great state of inner Africa, ruling the Dongola Reach above the Third Cataract. Its royal tumuli and deffufa temples mark a Nubian power that traded and fought with Egypt as an equal.

polities.name: Kingdom of Kush (Napata–Meroë)
polities.note: From Napata the Kushite kings conquered Egypt itself as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty; from Meroë they ruled a Nile empire of iron, cattle and royal pyramids for another thousand years, writing in their own Meroitic script.

polities.name: Carthage
polities.note: A Phoenician colony that became the merchant empire of the western Mediterranean, commanding the African shore from the Gulf of Sirte to the Atlantic until Rome razed it in the Third Punic War.

polities.name: Numidia
polities.note: The Berber kingdom of Masinissa and Jugurtha, famed for its cavalry, which unified the Maghrib interior between Carthaginian coast and Saharan fringe before falling into Rome's orbit.

polities.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
polities.note: The Macedonian dynasty of the Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Greek Alexandria, whose library and lighthouse made it the intellectual capital of the Hellenistic world, until Cleopatra's fleet broke at Actium.
sources: Hölbl, History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)

polities.name: Roman North Africa
polities.note: Rome's granary. From Mauretania to Cyrenaica the provinces of Africa fed the imperial capital with wheat and olive oil, raised amphitheatres at El Djem and Leptis, and gave the empire Septimius Severus and Augustine.

polities.name: Kingdom of Aksum
polities.note: The trading empire of the northern Horn, minting its own gold coinage, raising granite stelae, and adopting Christianity in the fourth century - counted by Mani among the four great powers of the world.
sources: Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation (2012)

polities.name: Makuria
polities.note: The greatest of the Christian Nubian kingdoms, whose baqt treaty with Islamic Egypt held the frontier at Aswan for six centuries - one of the longest-kept treaties in history - while cathedral frescoes bloomed at Faras.
sources: Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002)

polities.name: Alodia
polities.note: The southern Christian kingdom of Nubia, ruling from Soba on the Blue Nile over the Gezira plains; travellers reported gold-roofed churches before it fell to Funj and Arab pressure.

polities.name: Ghana (Wagadu)
polities.note: The first recorded empire of the western Sudan, called the land of gold by Arab geographers: Soninke kings taxed the desert caravans that exchanged Saharan salt for Bambuk gold.

polities.name: Mali Empire
polities.note: Founded by Sundiata after Kirina and made legend by Mansa Musa, whose hajj of 1324 spent so much gold that Cairo's market was depressed for years. At its height Mali ruled the Niger from the Atlantic to Gao, with Timbuktu as its university city.

polities.name: Songhai Empire
polities.note: Under Sunni Ali's river fleet and Askia Muhammad's administration, Songhai became the largest empire in African history to that point, ruling the Niger bend until Moroccan muskets broke it at Tondibi.
sources: Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire (1999)

polities.name: Kanem Empire
polities.note: The Saharan empire northeast of Lake Chad, whose Sefuwa mais embraced Islam in the eleventh century and ran the central caravan road to Fezzan and Tripoli on horses and slaves.
sources: Lange, Kingdoms and Peoples of Chad (1984)

polities.name: Bornu Empire
polities.note: Kanem reborn west of Lake Chad. Under Mai Idris Alooma it fielded chain-mailed cavalry and Ottoman muskets, and its dynasty - the Sefuwa - ranks among the longest-reigning in world history.

polities.name: Almoravid Empire
polities.note: A Sanhaja Berber reform movement out of the western Sahara that founded Marrakesh and welded Morocco, the Sahara road and al-Andalus into one empire of the veil.

polities.name: Almohad Caliphate
polities.note: The Masmuda Berber caliphate that unified the whole Maghrib from Atlantic to Tripoli - the only power ever to do so from within - and built the Koutoubia and Giralda minarets.

polities.name: Fatimid Caliphate
polities.note: An Ismaili dynasty that rose in Ifriqiya, conquered Egypt and founded Cairo and al-Azhar, ruling a Mediterranean and Red Sea trading empire in rivalry with Baghdad.

polities.name: Mamluk Sultanate
polities.note: The slave-soldier sultanate that stopped the Mongols at Ayn Jalut and expelled the Crusaders, making Cairo the largest city outside China and the seat of the Abbasid caliphs in exile.

polities.name: Zagwe Kingdom
polities.note: The Agaw dynasty of highland Ethiopia whose king Lalibela had eleven churches hewn from living rock as a new Jerusalem - still in liturgical use today.

polities.name: Ethiopian Empire (Solomonic)
polities.note: The dynasty claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba ruled the highlands for seven centuries, repelled Ahmad Gragn with Portuguese help, built castles at Gondar, and alone in Africa crushed a European coloniser at Adwa in 1896.

polities.name: Adal Sultanate
polities.note: The Muslim sultanate of the eastern Horn whose imam, Ahmad Gragn, swept across the Ethiopian highlands in the 1530s with Ottoman firearms in one of the great wars of the sixteenth-century world.

polities.name: Ajuran Sultanate
polities.note: The hydraulic empire of the Horn: Ajuran engineers dug limestone wells and dammed the Shabelle, and its garrisons and fleet resisted Portuguese incursion on the Benadir coast.
sources: Cassanelli, The Shaping of Somali Society (1982)

polities.name: Kilwa Sultanate
polities.note: The queen of the Swahili coast, controlling the Sofala gold trade from a coral-stone city whose Great Mosque and Husuni Kubwa palace moved Ibn Battuta to call it among the most beautiful towns in the world.

polities.name: Mapungubwe
polities.note: Southern Africa's first state, at the Limpopo-Shashe confluence, where a gold-and-ivory trading elite was buried with the famous golden rhinoceros on a hilltop above the commoners' town.

polities.name: Great Zimbabwe
polities.note: The stone city of the Shona plateau - the largest ancient structure south of the Sahara, its Great Enclosure walled without mortar - grown rich on the cattle economy and the Sofala gold road.

polities.name: Mutapa Empire
polities.note: Heir to Great Zimbabwe on the northern plateau, whose mwene mutapa taxed the gold fairs of the Zambezi valley and drew Portuguese Sofala into vassalage games it never fully won.
sources: Mudenge, A Political History of Munhumutapa (1988)

polities.name: Rozvi Empire
polities.note: Changamire Dombo's warrior state drove the Portuguese from the plateau in the 1690s - the first African army to expel a European power from conquered territory - and ruled from stone courts at Danangombe.

polities.name: Kingdom of Kongo
polities.note: The centralised kingdom at the Congo's mouth that exchanged ambassadors with Lisbon and the Vatican, converted to Christianity under its own kings, and fought the Atlantic slave trade's corrosion of its provinces for three centuries.

polities.name: Ife
polities.note: The sacred city of the Yoruba, whose naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads rank with any portraiture on earth, and from whose dynasty the crowned kings of Yorubaland trace descent.
sources: Blier, Art and Risk in Ancient Yoruba (2015)

polities.name: Kingdom of Benin
polities.note: The Edo kingdom whose obas cast the Benin Bronzes, ringed their capital with earthworks longer than any other in the world, and traded with Portugal as equals until the British punitive expedition of 1897.

polities.name: Oyo Empire
polities.note: The savanna empire of the Yoruba, whose cavalry - unique in the forest belt's shadow - made vassals of Dahomey and whose alafin governed through the checks of the Oyo Mesi council.

polities.name: Hausa City-States
polities.note: The seven walled cities of Hausaland - Kano, Katsina, Zazzau and their sisters - ran the southern terminals of the Saharan trade, weaving and dyeing cloth whose indigo reached Timbuktu and Tripoli.

polities.name: Ashanti Empire
polities.note: Founded when Osei Tutu received the Golden Stool from the sky as the soul of the nation, Asante built a gold-weighted bureaucratic empire that fought the British to a standstill four times in the nineteenth century.
sources: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

polities.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
polities.note: The disciplined kingdom of the Fon, ruled from the storied palaces of Abomey, whose standing army included the famous women soldiers Europeans called Amazons.

polities.name: Sokoto Caliphate
polities.note: Usman dan Fodio's jihad forged the largest state in nineteenth-century Africa: thirty emirates from Burkina to Cameroon under the caliph at Sokoto, a scholarly empire whose poets included his daughter Nana Asmaʼu.

polities.name: Funj Sultanate of Sennar
polities.note: The Black Sultanate of the Blue Nile, which absorbed Christian Alodia, islamised the Gezira, and for three centuries brokered gold, gum and pilgrims between Ethiopia, Egypt and the Red Sea.
sources: O'Fahey & Spaulding, Kingdoms of the Sudan (1974)

polities.name: Sultanate of Darfur
polities.note: The Fur sultanate of the Marra massif, master of the Forty Days Road to Egypt, whose keira dynasty ruled a layered court of titled officials until Zubayr's conquest.

polities.name: Wadai Sultanate
polities.note: The Maba sultanate east of Lake Chad that threw off Darfur, opened its own desert road to Benghazi, and was the last of the great Sudanic states to fall to European conquest.

polities.name: Bagirmi Sultanate
polities.note: The Barma kingdom southeast of Lake Chad, squeezed between Bornu and Wadai, whose mbang held court at Massenya behind walls of sun-dried brick.
sources: Lange, Kingdoms and Peoples of Chad (1984)

polities.name: Luba Empire
polities.note: The savanna empire of the upper Congo whose kings ruled through the memory of the lukasa - beaded boards encoding history - and whose model of sacred kingship seeded states across Central Africa.
sources: Reefe, The Rainbow and the Kings (1981)

polities.name: Lunda Empire
polities.note: From the court of the mwant yav, Lunda's system of positional succession let it franchise kingship across a third of Central Africa, tying Atlantic and East African trade into one network.

polities.name: Buganda
polities.note: The lake kingdom whose kabakas ruled the most centralised court in the Great Lakes through appointed chiefs, banana wealth and a canoe navy on Victoria Nyanza.
sources: Reid, Political Power in Pre-Colonial Buganda (2002)

polities.name: Bunyoro-Kitara
polities.note: The elder kingdom of the Great Lakes, heir to the Chwezi earthworks, whose omukamas controlled the salt of Kibiro and the ivory roads west of the Nile until Buganda and Britain hemmed it in.
sources: Nyakatura, Anatomy of an African Kingdom (1973)

polities.name: Kingdom of Rwanda
polities.note: The tightly-woven hill kingdom of the mwami, whose court poetry, cattle clientage and standing armies made it among the most centralised polities in Africa on the eve of colonisation.

polities.name: Zulu Kingdom
polities.note: Shaka's military revolution - the short stabbing spear, the age-regiment, the horns of the buffalo - forged a kingdom whose army destroyed a British column at Isandlwana in 1879.

polities.name: Basotho Kingdom
polities.note: Moshoeshoe gathered the survivors of the wars of the Mfecane onto the mountain of night, holding off Boer and British arms by diplomacy as much as war and preserving a nation that endures as Lesotho.

polities.name: Ndebele Kingdom
polities.note: Mzilikazi led his people a thousand miles north from Zululand through the Mfecane to found a new kingdom on the plateau, ruled through Zulu-style regiments until Rhodes's Maxim guns came.

polities.name: Merina Kingdom
polities.note: From the highland rice terraces Andrianampoinimerina and Radama I unified most of Madagascar, importing schools and industry while the rova palace crowned Antananarivo, until the French conquest of 1895–97.
sources: Campbell, An Economic History of Imperial Madagascar (2005)

polities.name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
polities.note: When Sayyid Said moved his court from Muscat, Zanzibar became the clove garden and entrepôt of the western Indian Ocean - and the hub of a caravan and slave-trade network reaching the Congo.
sources: Sheriff, Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar (1987)

polities.name: Toucouleur Empire
polities.note: Al-Hajj Umar Tal's Tijani jihad swept from Futa Toro to the Niger, taking Segou and Masina, and left his son Ahmadu to face the French columns with the Sudan's last great army.
sources: Robinson, The Holy War of Umar Tal (1985)

polities.name: Massina Empire
polities.note: Seku Amadu's Fulbe theocracy of the inner Niger delta, which regulated the annual cattle crossings, veiled Timbuktu's taverns, and built a capital of scholars at Hamdullahi.

polities.name: Wassoulou Empire
polities.note: Samori Touré built the last empire of the western Sudan with home-forged rifles and a mobile state that fought the French for sixteen years - the longest resistance war of the Scramble.

polities.name: Imamate of Futa Jallon
polities.note: The Fulbe imamate of the Guinea highlands, one of the first jihad states of West Africa, whose alternating almami and provincial councils ran a federation famous for its Qurʼanic schools.
sources: Barry, Senegambia and the Atlantic Slave Trade (1998)

polities.name: Akwamu
polities.note: The Akan empire of the Gold Coast's eastern trade paths, which held Accra's European forts to ransom and whose statecraft Asante later absorbed and surpassed.

polities.name: Kaabu Empire
polities.note: Mali's western province turned independent Mandinka empire between the Gambia and Corubal rivers, ruled by nyancho warrior lineages until Futa Jallon's cavalry burned Kansala.

polities.name: Jolof Empire
polities.note: The Wolof empire between the Senegal and Gambia rivers, a federation of five vassal kingdoms under the buurba, that fractured when Atlantic trade pulled its coastal provinces away.

polities.name: Egypt of Muhammad Ali
polities.note: The Albanian officer who seized Ottoman Egypt built conscript armies, cotton monoculture and Nile-to-Sudan conquests into the Middle East's first industrialising state, before European debt brought the British occupation.
